nameStory: The 'tickseed' name comes from the plant's small, dark seeds that look remarkably like tiny ticks clinging to your clothes or pet's fur. The 'large-flowered' part distinguishes this species from its smaller cousins - these sunny blooms can reach up to 2-3 inches across, making them the showstoppers of the tickseed family.
description: Large-flowered tickseed is a cheerful perennial wildflower that brightens prairies and gardens with brilliant golden-yellow daisy-like blooms. This sturdy plant grows up to 2 feet tall or more, sending up multiple flower stems from a central base. Each flower head features bright yellow petals (technically ray flowers) surrounding a darker yellow center packed with tiny disc flowers. It's a native prairie plant that's equally at home in wild meadows and cultivated flower beds.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright golden-yellow daisy-like blooms up to 2-3 inches across with 8 broad, notched petals that feel papery to the touch and surround a darker yellow center

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, lance-shaped leaves that feel slightly rough and may be deeply lobed or divided, growing opposite each other on the stem

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Upright perennial growing 1-2+ feet tall with multiple branching flower stems arising from a central base, creating a bushy appearance

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Small, dark, oval seeds that look like tiny ticks and feel hard and smooth when rubbed between your fingers

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Slender, branching stems that feel smooth to slightly rough and often have a reddish tinge, especially near the base

habitat: In New England, large-flowered tickseed is quite rare in the wild, with only one documented observation, likely because it's primarily a prairie species more at home in the Midwest. When found, it prefers open, sunny locations like meadows, field edges, roadsides, or disturbed ground with well-drained soil. You're most likely to encounter it in gardens, where it's commonly cultivated, or as an occasional escape from cultivation.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as rosettes of narrow leaves at ground level, with flower stems beginning to develop in late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season from early to late summer, producing waves of bright yellow flowers that attract bees and butterflies. Deadheading spent blooms encourages continued flowering.
seasonality.fall: Later flowers continue blooming into early fall, followed by seed development. Plants begin to decline as temperatures drop and seeds ripen for dispersal.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground portions die back completely, leaving only dormant roots underground. Old seed heads may persist, appearing as dry, brown stalks.

funFact: This humble wildflower is such a garden superstar that it's conquered China - originally from North American prairies, it's now widely cultivated and naturalized across China, where it's become a beloved ornamental plant in parks and gardens thousands of miles from its prairie home.
confusionNotes: Large-flowered tickseed can be confused with other yellow daisy-like flowers, especially black-eyed Susan, but tickseed has a yellow center (not dark brown) and more delicate, notched petals. Remember: 'Tickseed has a sunny yellow center to match its sunny disposition, while black-eyed Susan literally has black eyes.'
contextualKnowledge: Despite being native to North America, large-flowered tickseed is extremely rare as a wild plant in New England - you're far more likely to see it in someone's garden than growing wild. Most 'wild' populations here are actually garden escapes rather than truly native stands.
compareHints: Large-flowered tickseed stands out from other New England tickseeds by its size - both the flowers and overall plant are notably larger than rose coreopsis (which has pink flowers) or lance-leaved coreopsis. The flowers are broader and showier than whorled coreopsis, and unlike plains coreopsis, the petals are solid yellow without reddish markings at the base.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Rose Coreopsis is the only tickseed in New England with pink or white petals - all its relatives like Lance-leaved and Whorled Coreopsis have bright yellow flowers.
Among its tickseed relatives, Whorled Coreopsis is the only one with thread-like leaves arranged in distinct whorls around the stem.

Lance-leaved Coreopsis differs from other Coreopsis species by its simple, unlobed lance-shaped leaves - Rose Coreopsis has much smaller pink flowers, while Whorled Coreopsis has very finely divided, thread-like leaves.
Plains coreopsis differs from other New England coreopsis species by being an annual (dies each year) rather than perennial, and by having the most deeply divided, feathery leaves of the group.
Tall coreopsis dwarfs all other New England coreopsis species - most relatives like lance-leaved coreopsis and rose coreopsis stay under 3 feet tall.

Among New England's coreopsis species, lobed coreopsis is immediately distinguished by its uniquely shaped leaves - rose coreopsis has narrow linear leaves, lance-leaved has simple spear-shaped leaves, and whorled coreopsis has thread-like leaves in circles around the stem.

Unlike its New England relatives like Lance-leaved Coreopsis (which has simple, narrow leaves) or Rose Coreopsis (which has thin, needle-like leaves), Prairie Coreopsis has those distinctive deeply-divided, finger-like leaves that make it unmistakable.
